analysis.one_liner: Limits how many patents brand-name biologic drugmakers can use to sue copycat competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cap patent lawsuits against biosimilar makers, was referred to three House committees in July 2024, moved to a Health subcommittee in December, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name biologic drug (a protein-based medicine made from living cells, like an arthritis or cancer biologic) is about to lose exclusivity, its maker can sue the copycat 'biosimilar' competitor and drag out litigation with dozens of patents. This bill would cap how many patents the brand-name maker can assert in that lawsuit — generally 20, with tighter limits on patents filed long after the original drug was approved — making it cheaper and faster to bring lower-cost biosimilars to market. It also directs $1.8 billion into the Medicare Improvement Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs. Biosimilar competition typically brings prices down substantially, and the bill removes a key delay tactic — patent-thicket litigation — that brand-name makers use to keep cheaper versions off the market. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly through lower Medicare and Medicaid drug spending.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the patents a brand-name biologic sponsor can assert in an infringement suit against a biosimilar applicant at 20, with no more than 10 of them being patents that issued more than four years after the original drug's approval [S2].
Lets a court expand the cap only for good cause, with limits designed to stop sponsors from stacking late-filed patents onto a single lawsuit [S2].
Extends infringement findings so biosimilar litigation reaches patents claiming the biologic itself, its uses, and its manufacture, which consolidates rather than fragments the patent fight [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, whose main tactic for delaying biosimilar competitors — asserting dozens of overlapping patents in court — would be curtailed, shortening their period of monopoly pricing.

drawbacks.text: The cap has exceptions: courts can raise the number of patents for good cause, and the limit does not apply to method-of-treatment patents, so determined sponsors retain ways to stretch litigation [S2].
The bill sets the Medicare Improvement Fund at $1.8 billion, federal spending whose offset depends on the savings from faster biosimilar entry actually materializing [S2].

Drugmakers and some patent advocates argue that limiting patent enforcement weakens incentives to invest in biologic development, where products are costly to invent and hard to copy; this bill restricts only one enforcement pathway, not the patents themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real but modest by design: the bill attacks one delay tactic — patent stacking in litigation — without touching the underlying patents, and its exceptions give courts room to waive the cap. An honest supporter would concede it narrows rather than ends the product-hopping problem, but even a partial curb on patent thickets lowers costs for patients on biologics, whose prices are among the highest in medicine.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat with three House committees after referral in July 2024, got only a routine December referral to a Health subcommittee, and died when the 118th Congress ended without ever reaching a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) introduced the bill on July 18, 2024, joined by Rep. Johnson of Georgia, and it was referred to the Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce committees [S1][S2][S4].
The bill had bipartisan sponsorship, with two House Democrats listed as cosponsors [S3].
On December 17, 2024, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health — the last action in the record [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers are better off: with no vote ever taken, they keep the ability to assert large numbers of patents against biosimilar challengers, and patients continue paying brand-name prices for longer. The bipartisan sponsors lost their attempt to speed up biosimilar competition.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill and two Democrats cosponsored it; no recorded opposition exists in the congressional record, so the partisan shape of the lack of action is unclear.

industries.note: Their principal tool for delaying biosimilar competition — asserting large numbers of patents, many filed years after approval, in litigation — would be capped at 20 patents per suit. Blocking or burying this bill preserves their monopoly pricing window on some of the most expensive drugs patients take.
A tighter patent cap shortens litigation, lowers the cost of challenging brand-name biologics, and gets lower-priced biosimilars to market sooner — the same outcome patients want.
